client: I've been really struggling since my partner passed away six months ago from cancer. Everything just feels kind of gray and empty, and I don't find myself enjoying things I used to love at all. I've also been pulling away from friends, and honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change any of that.
therapist: I'm so deeply sorry for the loss of your partner — what you're carrying right now is profound, and the grayness and emptiness you're describing make complete sense after such a devastating loss. It takes real courage to show up here even when a part of you doubts it will help, and I want you to know that doubt is welcome here too. I'm curious — when you imagine what "feeling better" might even look like, does any small flicker of what that could be come to mind, or does it feel completely out of reach right now?

client: Honestly, "feeling better" feels almost like a betrayal somehow — like if I stop hurting this much, it means I've moved on and forgotten them, which I don't ever want to do. Sometimes I get a tiny flicker, like maybe one day I could go back to hiking, which we used to do together, but then it's immediately followed by this wave of guilt. It's hard to even hold onto that flicker without it turning into something painful.
therapist: What you just shared is so important — the idea that healing feels like betrayal is one of the most common and painful thoughts people carry after losing someone they deeply loved, and it makes so much sense that your mind would try to protect that bond this way. But I'd gently invite you to consider: is it possible that carrying them with you *into* that hiking trail someday might actually be a way of honoring them, rather than leaving them behind? What do you think your partner would say if they could see you standing at the trailhead again?

client: I know logically they would probably want me to keep hiking, they were always the one pushing me to get outside even when I didn't feel like it. But knowing that and actually feeling okay about it are two completely different things — it's like my head and my heart are speaking different languages right now. And honestly, the idea of being on that trail without them just sounds incredibly lonely, not healing.
therapist: That gap between knowing something and truly *feeling* it is one of the most honest and human experiences there is, and you've described it beautifully — your heart is grieving on its own timeline, and that deserves real respect. The loneliness you're anticipating on that trail is real too, and I don't want to rush past it, because sometimes what feels like an obstacle is actually pointing us toward something important we need. I wonder — when you imagine being on that trail and feeling that loneliness, what do you think you'd most need in that moment to feel even the tiniest bit less alone?

client: Maybe having another person there, someone who actually knew them, so I wouldn't have to explain the weight of it — but then I think about reaching out to any of our mutual friends and I just freeze up. I've been pulling away so much that it feels like too much time has passed now, like it would be awkward or they'd think I'm finally "over it" and want to talk about moving on. I guess I'm scared of being misunderstood, or worse, of breaking down in front of someone and making them uncomfortable.
therapist: The fear of being misunderstood or becoming "too much" for someone else to handle is such a vulnerable place to be, and it makes sense that pulling away has felt safer than risking that hurt on top of everything else you're already carrying. But I want to gently reflect something back — those mutual friends lost someone too, and there's a real chance they might be waiting, maybe even freezing up in their own way, wondering if *you* want to hear their name spoken aloud. What do you imagine might happen if one of them knew exactly how you just described this — not that you're "over it," but that you're scared of being misunderstood?

client: That actually made me stop and think for a second, because you're right that they lost them too, and I haven't really let myself think about it from their side. But even imagining sending a text to one of them right now makes my chest tighten up — what do I even say after six months of silence? I wouldn't even know where to start, and I'm worried that whatever I say will come out wrong and just make everything more awkward than it already is.
therapist: That tightening in your chest is worth listening to — it's telling you this matters deeply to you, not that you shouldn't do it. And here's something worth considering: after six months of shared grief, a message as simple as "I've been thinking about you and missing them" might land far more gently than you'd expect, because it's just the truth. Would you be open to sitting with one person's name in your mind this week — not committing to sending anything yet, just noticing what comes up when you imagine it?

client: I think I can probably manage just sitting with a name without having to actually do anything yet — that feels slightly less terrifying than committing to sending a message. There's one person, my partner's closest friend from college, who I keep almost texting and then talking myself out of, so maybe it's them. I just worry that even letting myself think about it will stir everything up and then I'll have to sit with all that feeling alone, with no way to make it stop.
therapist: It means a lot that you already have someone in mind, and the fact that you keep *almost* reaching for that connection tells me a part of you is ready, even while another part is protecting you. The fear of stirring up feelings with no way to make them stop is so real — but I want to gently offer that sitting with those feelings, even painfully, is actually how grief slowly loses some of its sharp edges over time, and you wouldn't have to navigate that completely alone if we're here working through it together. When those waves of feeling have come up in the past six months, what has helped you get through to the other side of them, even just a little?

client: Honestly, the things that have helped most are pretty small and almost embarrassing to admit — like making a cup of tea, or putting on a documentary late at night just to have some noise in the apartment. They don't really fix anything, they just kind of get me through the next hour until the wave passes. I'm not sure if that counts as coping or just avoiding, but it's what I've got right now.
therapist: Those small things are not embarrassing at all — they're actually a quiet form of wisdom your nervous system has figured out on its own, and "getting through the next hour" is a completely legitimate and meaningful form of survival. There's an important difference between avoiding feelings permanently and simply giving yourself a gentle bridge to carry you through the most intense moments, and what you're describing sounds much more like the latter. I'm curious — when you're sitting with that tea or that documentary and the wave starts to ease, do you ever notice any small trace of your partner in those quiet moments, or does it mostly just feel like getting through?

client: Actually, yes — they were the one who got me into documentaries in the first place, so sometimes when I'm watching one I'll have this split-second reflex to turn and say something to them about it, and then remember. It's this horrible little jolt, but underneath it there's also something that feels almost like they're still there for just a moment, which is confusing because I don't know if that's comforting or just making things worse. I've never really let myself sit with that long enough to figure out which one it is.
therapist: What you just described — that split-second where they're almost there in the room with you — sounds less like a wound and more like a thread that still connects you to them, and I don't think it has to be either purely comforting or purely painful; it can be both at once, and that complexity is actually a sign of how real and deep your love was. Those moments might even be worth gently protecting rather than rushing past, because they seem to carry something meaningful that your grief hasn't swallowed yet. I wonder — if you allowed yourself to sit with that feeling just a little longer next time instead of pulling away from the jolt, what do you imagine you might find on the other side of it?

client: I honestly don't know what I'd find, and that uncertainty is part of what makes it scary — it feels like stepping off a ledge without knowing how far the drop is. Part of me thinks I might just completely fall apart, and unlike the tea or the documentary, I'm not sure I'd be able to pull myself back from that. I want to believe there's something meaningful on the other side like you're saying, but I'm not convinced I'm strong enough to handle it yet.
therapist: The fear that you might fall apart and not be able to return is one of the most honest things you've shared, and I want to sit with that for a moment rather than rush to reassure you — because it deserves real respect, not a quick "you'll be fine." But I also want to gently reflect something back: you have already survived six months of one of the hardest things a person can go through, finding small ways to carry yourself through each wave, and that is not nothing — that is actually evidence of a quiet strength that's been there all along, even when it doesn't feel like it. What do you think it would take for you to start trusting that strength just a little more than you do right now?

client: I think part of what would help is having some kind of proof that I've actually made it through the hard moments, because right now my memory just kind of blurs all six months together into one long gray stretch and I can't really distinguish the times I survived from the times I just went numb. It's hard to trust a strength I can't actually see or point to. Maybe if I could somehow recognize it in the moment rather than just being told it's there, it would feel more real to me.
therapist: What you're describing is such a clear and self-aware insight — you don't need someone to tell you the strength is there, you need to be able to *see* it for yourself, and that's a completely reasonable thing to want. One small thing that sometimes helps is keeping a very simple record — even just a few words on your phone when you notice you've made it through a hard moment, not to analyze it, just to make it visible so the gray stretch starts to have some shape and texture. Would you be open to trying something like that this week — just noticing and naming one moment where you got through, even if it was just the tea and the documentary?
